transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I suppose what brings me in is that my sleep has become completely unmoored. It's strange how it shifts. At first, I was up after just two or three hours, drafting plans and feeling completely ready to go. I was actually mapping out a massive project to index all my old university research—I have boxes of it in the study from my graduate days. Back then, we didn't have digital archives, you know, it was all physical paper and microfiche. God, the smell of that library, it was like old leather and dust. I used to know the head librarian, Margaret, wonderful woman, always wore these heavy wool cardigans... 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. The sleep. It's not like that anymore. Now... now I just lie awake before dawn with my stomach tight and no sense of rest at all. I just watch the light change on the ceiling. The streetlights outside my window have this awful orange glow to them. They switched them to LED a few years back and it completely ruined the aesthetic of the neighborhood, honestly. But yes, the sleep is just gone.
Have you been feeling unusually happy or energetic lately?

Well, for a few weeks there, I felt... brilliantly optimistic, I'd say. Energetic doesn't quite cover it. It was like every obstacle in the world was completely trivial, just dust to be brushed away. I felt like I could accomplish anything. I actually started looking into buying a sailboat. I haven't sailed since I was in my thirties, down off the coast of Maine. The water there is freezing, even in August, but the wind... you catch a good breeze and it's like flying. My old friend Arthur had a schooner, beautiful wooden hull, teak decks that we had to oil every season. He moved to Florida eventually, couldn't take the winters. I don't blame him, really, the snow shoveling alone at our age is a heart attack waiting to happen. 

But yes, I was feeling incredibly capable. Though, I have to admit, if anyone questioned my plans—like my daughter, who was terribly unsupportive about the boat—I just snapped at them. I felt like they were trying to sabotage me. Like I was the only sensible man in the room and everyone else was just dragging their feet. It was infuriating, honestly, dealing with people who just couldn't see the vision.
Are you currently feeling sad or empty most of the time?

Sad? Empty? No... no, I wouldn't say that. I don't really feel much of anything right now, to be honest. It's more like a... a heaviness. Like I'm just sitting at the bottom of a very deep well. It reminds me of this old well we had on the property when I was a boy. My grandfather built it—brick by brick, he always used to say. He was a mason, you know. Came over from Scotland in the twenties. He had these massive hands, rough as sandpaper, but he could do the most delicate stonework. He built this beautiful retaining wall around the garden that's probably still standing today. They don't build things to last anymore, do they? Everything is just cheap plastic and planned obsolescence. I bought a toaster last year and it broke within a month. A month! Can you believe that? The one I had before that lasted fifteen years. 

But no, I'm not... I wouldn't call it sad. Just... waiting, I suppose.
Do you feel guilty about anything?

Guilty? Yes... yes, I suppose I do. It's this one thing, doctor, it just goes round and round in my head. I keep replaying this investment decision I made. I convinced myself it was brilliant during that... that energetic phase. Now I just look at it and think I've completely ruined my wife's security. It's agonizing. I've spent my whole life being the responsible one, you know? The one everyone relies on. I was a financial analyst for thirty-five years. Thirty-five years! I started back when we used ledger paper and adding machines. You had to really know your numbers then, you couldn't just rely on a spreadsheet to do the math for you. My first boss, Mr. Henderson, he was a stickler for neat handwriting. If your sevens didn't have a cross through them, he'd make you do the whole page over. He was tough, but fair. He actually retired to Arizona, bought a little place near Sedona. Have you ever been to Sedona? The red rocks there, especially at sunset, they're just magnificent. It's supposed to be some sort of energy vortex, though I never really bought into all that New Age nonsense. People will believe anything if you package it right, won't they? Just look at all these fad diets...

But yes, I feel like an absolute fool. I've jeopardized everything we built, and for what?
How long did this energetic and optimistic phase last?

Well, the energetic part... the part where I thought I was invincible... that was just a few weeks. But the aftermath? That's what really consumed me. For about five months after the investment loss, I wasn't living like my usual retired self at all. Everything, and I mean everything, revolved around trying to undo the damage. I was obsessed. 

I'd sit at my desk for hours, pouring over the same financial reports, trying to find a loophole, a way out. It reminded me of when I was working on my master's thesis back in '78. I spent an entire semester practically living in the university library. It was this beautiful old Gothic building, stained glass windows, smelled like old paper and floor wax. The librarian, Mrs. Gable, she used to sneak me cups of coffee in the back room because you weren't allowed to have drinks near the stacks. She was a sweetheart, had this enormous orange cat that used to sleep on the card catalog. You don't see card catalogs anymore, do you? It's a shame. There was something satisfying about flipping through those little cards, the physical act of finding information. Now it's all just typing into a search bar. It feels so... disconnected. My grandson was showing me how he does research for school now on his tablet, and I just couldn't wrap my head around it. He swipes his finger and suddenly he has a hundred articles. Where's the effort? Where's the discovery? 

But yes, for five solid months, it was just me and the numbers, trying to fix a mess that couldn't be fixed.
Did you experience any periods where you didn't need much sleep and still felt rested?

Sleep? Yes, well, my sleep has become completely unmoored, doctor. That's actually a big part of what brings me in. At first, during that... that busy phase, I'd only sleep maybe two or three hours a night. I'd be up at 2 AM drafting all these elaborate plans, feeling absolutely ready to go. I had this big legal pad out—yellow paper, blue lines. I always buy the heavy-weight paper. You can't use a good fountain pen on cheap paper, it just bleeds right through the page. 

I have a Parker 51 fountain pen that my father gave me when I graduated with my master's. It's an aerometric fill, not those plastic disposable cartridges they use today. You have to actually dip the nib into a bottle of ink and squeeze the bar. There's a real art to it, a ritual. I use a lovely midnight blue ink from France. The bottle itself is a little glass work of art. I keep it on my desk next to this brass paperweight I bought in London... oh, maybe twenty years ago now? We took a trip there for our anniversary. Rained the entire time, of course, but the museums were spectacular. The British Museum... you could spend a month in there and not see everything. The Rosetta Stone is much smaller in person than you'd expect, though. 

But I'm sorry, you were asking about sleep. No, I don't feel rested anymore. Not at all. Now I just lie awake long before dawn, and my stomach is just... tight. Completely knotted up. There's no sense of rest whatsoever anymore, just me staring at the ceiling in the dark.
Did you make any impulsive decisions during that time when you felt brilliantly optimistic?

Impulsive decisions? Well, aside from that terrible investment, I don't... I don't really think so. No, nothing else comes to mind. But you know, speaking of decisions, it reminds me of when my wife and I decided to buy our first house. Oh, we looked for months. It was a completely different market back then, of course. Interest rates were sky-high in the early eighties. We ended up finding this charming little split-level on a cul-de-sac. It had these beautiful mature oak trees in the front yard. 

Oak trees are fascinating, really. Did you know they don't start producing acorns until they're about fifty years old? It's a lesson in patience. We had this one massive oak that would just blanket the driveway in acorns every fall. The squirrels were absolutely fearless. One of them—we called him Barnaby—used to come right up to the porch screen and chatter at our golden retriever, Max. Max was the sweetest dog, wouldn't hurt a fly, but he'd sit there and just whine at that squirrel for hours. We got Max from a rescue in... oh, it must have been '85. He had this funny little white patch on his chest that looked exactly like a bowtie. 

But no, doctor, to answer your question, I don't believe I did anything else impulsive like that. Just the investment.
Did you ever feel so irritable or impatient during those energetic weeks that you had difficulty controlling your temper?

Irritable? Well... it was a strange combination, really. Because for those weeks, I felt almost brilliantly optimistic. It was as if every obstacle in my path was completely trivial, just dust to be brushed away. But if anyone questioned me—even a simple, harmless question—I snapped at them. I treated them like they were deliberately trying to sabotage the only sensible man in the room. 

I remember snapping terribly at my wife when she came into the dining room to ask about lunch. I had all my papers spread out on the table. It's a gorgeous mahogany table, actually. We bought it at an estate sale back in... oh, 1998, I think. It belonged to a retired judge. Solid mahogany is so incredibly heavy, it took four grown men to get it through our front door. You have to be very careful with the finish, though. We always use these thick, felt-backed placemats if we set anything warm on it. My daughter bought us a beautiful set of those placemats from a little artisan market in Santa Fe. 

Have you ever been to New Mexico, doctor? The light out there... it's just different. The way it hits the mountains at sunset, it turns everything this incredible shade of violet and burnt orange. Georgia O'Keeffe spent years painting out there, and once you see the sky in person, you understand exactly why. She had that famous house in Abiquiu with the black patio door. People always think the desert is barren, but it's actually teeming with life if you just know where to look. 

But... anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yes, if anyone interrupted my train of thought or questioned what I was doing back then, I was incredibly impatient. Just furious with them for not seeing my vision.
Are you feeling hopeless about your future?

Hopeless? I... I don't know if hopeless is the right word. I just feel so incredibly heavy right now, like I can't see past the end of the day. But you know, thinking about the future reminds me of when I was finishing up my master's degree. I was so certain about how my life was going to unfold. I had everything mapped out. I was studying history—European history, specifically the interwar period. It's fascinating how much the world changed between 1918 and 1939. 

The League of Nations, for instance. Such a grand, optimistic idea that just completely fell apart. I actually spent a summer in Geneva doing research in their archives. The city is magnificent. The lake... Lake Geneva, or Lac Léman as the locals call it. It's so clear you can see right to the bottom in the shallows. And the Jet d'Eau, that massive fountain that shoots water hundreds of feet into the air. You can see it from almost anywhere in the city. I used to buy a fresh croissant from this tiny bakery near my flat and sit by the water every morning before heading to the archives. The baker was an older gentleman, missing half his left index finger. Never asked how it happened, but he made the most incredible pain au chocolat. The chocolate was always still slightly warm and gooey in the center. 

I haven't had a proper pastry like that in decades. Everything here is so mass-produced now, you know? It just comes out of a plastic wrapper. 

But... I'm sorry, you asked about the future. I just... I don't really know what to say about it right now. I just can't seem to look ahead at all.
Are you experiencing a loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed?

Loss of interest? Yes... yes, I suppose that's exactly what it is. I used to spend whole afternoons at the art museum downtown, just wandering the impressionist wing. Or I'd lose myself in photography. I had a whole darkroom set up in the basement at one point. Developing your own film is a dying art, you know. There's a real magic to watching an image slowly appear on the paper in the chemical bath under that red safety light. 

I actually bought my first real camera—a Leica M3—from a pawn shop in Chicago back in '78. It was a masterpiece of German engineering. The mechanics of it were so smooth, it was like winding a fine watch. I took it everywhere. I went to the Chicago World's Fair... well, not the famous one, but I went to an exposition there. Chicago is a remarkable city for architecture. Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House is down in Hyde Park. He designed everything, right down to the stained glass windows and the furniture, so the whole house was a single, unified work of art. They call it the Prairie School style. It's meant to echo the flat, expansive landscape of the Midwest. 

The Midwest is beautiful in its own way, especially in the autumn. The cornfields turn that dry, golden color, and the sky seems bigger somehow. We used to drive out to a pumpkin patch every October when my daughter was little. She always insisted on finding the absolute largest pumpkin in the field, even if it was completely misshapen. One year, we brought home this enormous, lopsided thing that barely fit in the trunk of the Volvo. Volvos were built like tanks back then. You felt like you could drive through a brick wall and not even scratch the bumper. 

But... oh, what were we talking about? Right, the museum and my hobbies. Yes, lately, I just... I look at my camera sitting on the shelf, or I think about cooking a nice meal, or even just sitting down at the bridge table, and I feel absolutely nothing. It's just... blank. The only thing I feel is how exhausting it would be to try and pretend I care.
How long have you been feeling this heaviness, like you're sitting at the bottom of a deep well?

Nine months, I suppose. Yes, it's been about nine months of this... this low, guilty withdrawal, ever since those big plans of mine completely fell apart. I had this grand idea, you see, to map out and write a book about the old abandoned railway lines in the county. The railways used to be the absolute lifeblood of this region. Back in the 1880s, the steam locomotives that came through here were true marvels of engineering. 

They used Baldwin engines, mostly. Baldwin Locomotive Works was based in Philadelphia, actually. Have you spent much time in Philadelphia, doctor? It's such a historically rich city. The masonry around Independence Hall... the Flemish bond brickwork is just exquisite. They simply don't lay brick like that anymore. Now it's all just cheap veneer over cinderblock. It completely lacks soul. 

I remember taking a walking tour of Philadelphia during the Bicentennial in '76. The crowds were absolutely enormous. Everyone was wearing those ridiculous tricorn hats. I bought a little felt one for my nephew. He was only four at the time, and he refused to take it off for a week. He even slept in it. Children have such wonderful, single-minded obsessions, don't they? They just latch onto something and the whole rest of the world just fades away. I wish I could still do that... just care about one simple thing like a felt hat. 

But... oh dear, I'm wandering again, aren't I? You asked about the heaviness. Yes. It's been about nine months since my plans collapsed and I just... sank into it.
Did you experience any periods where you felt abnormally elevated or irritable for most of the day?

Elevated? Oh, yes. Yes, before this terrible crash... for weeks, I felt almost brilliantly optimistic. It was as if every obstacle in the world was completely trivial, like I had cracked the code to life itself. I was so full of energy and grand ideas. But, you know, if anyone so much as questioned me or suggested I slow down, I would just snap at them. I treated them like they were trying to sabotage the only sensible man in the room. 

It reminds me of when I was working on a committee for the local historical society back in the late nineties. We were trying to preserve this old Victorian courthouse downtown. The architecture was stunning—Second Empire style, with that distinct mansard roof. You don't see true mansard roofs anymore. They were originally designed in France, you know, by François Mansart in the 17th century. It was a clever way to add an extra floor of living space without technically violating the zoning laws of Paris at the time. The French have always been so brilliantly subversive with their bureaucracy. 

I actually visited Paris with my late wife in 1985. We stayed in this tiny boutique hotel in the Marais district. The streets there are so narrow and winding, completely untouched by Haussmann's grand renovation of the city. We spent hours just walking, eating crepes from street vendors. She loved the ones with Nutella and banana. I always preferred the savory ones—ham and Gruyère cheese. The cheese over there just tastes different. It's unpasteurized, which I suppose makes it a bit dangerous by American standards, but the flavor is incredibly complex. 

But... I'm sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right. The irritability. Yes, I was terribly irritable if anyone got in my way during those energetic weeks. I just felt like I was moving at the speed of light and everyone else was standing still.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt sad or depressed most of the time?

Sad or depressed for two weeks? Well... I suppose I haven't really kept track of the exact number of weeks, to be perfectly honest. Time gets so blurry when you're sitting at home all day. I retired a few years ago, you see. I thought retirement was going to be this grand adventure. I had this whole list of books I was finally going to read. The complete works of Charles Dickens, for starters. 

Dickens was actually paid by the word, you know. That's why his novels are so incredibly long and descriptive. He originally published them as serials in magazines. People would line up at the docks in New York, waiting for the ships from England to arrive with the latest chapter of *The Old Curiosity Shop*. Can you imagine that? People caring that much about a story? Nowadays, everyone's just glued to their little screens, swiping through endless nonsense. There's no patience for a slow build-up anymore. 

I tried reading *Bleak House* last month, but I couldn't get past the first chapter. The fog in London... he describes it so perfectly, rolling down the Thames. The Thames used to be terribly polluted, you know. They called it the Great Stink in the summer of 1858. The smell of untreated sewage was so bad they actually had to hang curtains soaked in chloride of lime in the windows of Parliament just so they could conduct government business. 

But... what were you asking me? Oh, right, being sad for two weeks. I don't know about two weeks specifically. I just know it's been a long, awful stretch of feeling like this.
Have you had a period where you lost interest in almost all activities that you usually enjoyed?

Loss of interest? Yes... yes, absolutely. I used to spend whole afternoons down at the historical museum, or I'd completely lose myself in my photography. I had a whole darkroom set up in the basement. Developing film is such a lost art, really. The smell of the stop bath, the way the image just slowly ghosts onto the paper under the red light... it's pure magic. 

Silver gelatin prints, they call them. The silver halides in the emulsion react to the light. It's fascinating chemistry. I used to buy my chemicals from this little shop downtown that's been there since the fifties. The owner, Mr. Henderson, he knew everything there was to know about Leica cameras. Leicas are German, of course. The optics on their lenses are just unparalleled. Henri Cartier-Bresson used a Leica. He was the master of the "decisive moment," you know. He'd just wait for hours on a street corner until all the elements in the frame aligned perfectly. 

I tried to explain that concept to my niece when she was taking pictures with her phone at a family reunion, but she just put a filter on it and called it a day. The younger generation, they just want instant gratification. Everything is digital, everything is disposable. There's no permanence anymore. We used to print our photos and put them in heavy leather albums. Now they just float around in the "cloud." What happens when the servers go down? What happens to all those memories? 

Oh, dear, I've done it again, haven't I? I'm sorry, doctor. You asked about losing interest. Yes. It's just... lately, I look at my camera, or I think about going to the bridge table or even cooking a nice meal, and I feel absolutely nothing. Nothing at all, except just... the sheer, exhausting effort it would take to even pretend I care.
Are you unable to experience pleasure from activities that you once found enjoyable?

Pleasure? Yes, I suppose that's exactly what I was just getting at. There's just no joy in it anymore. Like I mentioned, I used to lose myself in those afternoons at the museum, or cooking a really elaborate meal. 

I used to make a phenomenal Beef Wellington. It's a tremendously difficult dish to get right, you know. The trick is the mushroom duxelles—you have to cook all the moisture out of the mushrooms, or else it completely ruins the puff pastry. Puff pastry is a marvel of culinary engineering. The French call it *mille-feuille*, a thousand leaves. It's just alternating layers of dough and butter, folded over and over. When it bakes, the water in the butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart. You really need a high-fat European butter for it. American butter has too much water. I used to go to this wonderful little specialty grocer on 4th Street just for the butter. The fellow who ran it always tried to sell me on these expensive white truffles from Alba. Truffle hunting is fascinating. They used to use pigs, you know, but the pigs would always try to eat the truffles, so they had to switch to specially trained dogs... 

Oh, dear. I'm drifting again, aren't I? I apologize. But to answer your question... no. No pleasure at all. Just like I said a moment ago, I look at my camera, or I think about sitting down at the bridge table, and I feel absolutely nothing. There's no spark. Just the heavy, exhausting realization of how much effort it would take to even pretend I'm having a good time.
Have you had a period of two weeks or more where you felt depressed or sad nearly every day?

Well, as I was saying earlier... two weeks, specifically? I couldn't tell you the exact calendar days. It's just been a very long, very gray time. I haven't been marking off the days on a calendar like a prisoner. 

Speaking of calendars, did you know the Gregorian calendar we use today was actually introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582? It was a reform of the Julian calendar, which Julius Caesar put into place. The Julian calendar was slightly inaccurate because it calculated the solar year as exactly 365.25 days, which is just a tiny bit too long. Over the centuries, the dates of the equinoxes started drifting, which was a huge problem for the Church because they needed to calculate the date of Easter accurately. So, they had to skip ten days in October of 1582 just to get everything back on track. People went to sleep on October 4th and woke up on October 15th. Imagine the confusion! Of course, Protestant countries refused to adopt it for hundreds of years just because it came from a Pope. England didn't switch over until 1752, and by then they had to skip eleven days. There were riots in the streets, people shouting, "Give us our eleven days!" 

It's fascinating how we try to measure and contain time, isn't it? But when you feel like this... when the sadness just settles over you like a heavy wool blanket... time doesn't really matter. It just drags on. So, two weeks? I don't know. It feels like forever.
Are you unable to find pleasure in activities that normally bring you happiness?

Well, doctor, I feel like we're going in circles a bit, aren't we? I thought I just answered that, but... yes. The pleasure is completely gone. 

I was just mentioning the photography and the museum, and the cooking. The bridge table, too. Bridge is such an elegant game. It requires so much concentration and partnership. It's not like poker, which is all bluffing and deceit. Bridge is about communication. You have to signal your partner with your bids, tell them what you hold without actually saying it. Contract bridge, the version we play now, was invented by Harold Vanderbilt in the 1920s while he was on a cruise through the Panama Canal. He just took the older game of auction bridge and refined the scoring. The Vanderbilts, of course, made their fortune in railroads and shipping. Cornelius Vanderbilt started with just one little ferry boat in New York Harbor and built an empire. They built those massive, ostentatious mansions in Newport, Rhode Island, just for the summer season. The Breakers, they called one of them. Imagine having a house like that just for a few weeks a year...

But yes, to your question... I just don't have the energy for it. I look at the cards, or my camera, and I just feel... empty. The thought of even trying to enjoy it, trying to participate and pretend I care... it's just too much effort. There's no happiness to be found in any of it right now.
Have you felt this heavy, empty feeling for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Well, yes, most of the day, every day... it's been about nine months now. Ever since those big plans of mine completely fell apart, I've just been in this low, guilty sort of withdrawal. 

Nine months is a significant amount of time, isn't it? It's the gestation period for a human being. It's fascinating how the human body just knows exactly how long to take to form a person. Elephants, on the other hand, are pregnant for nearly two years. Almost 22 months! Can you imagine carrying that kind of weight for that long? And baby elephants are born weighing around 250 pounds. They can stand up almost immediately, which is an evolutionary necessity on the savanna, of course. If they couldn't walk right away, they'd be easy prey for lions or hyenas. Hyenas are actually incredibly misunderstood creatures. People think they're just scavengers, but they are actually highly successful hunters. They have one of the strongest bite forces in the mammalian kingdom, strong enough to crush bone. They live in these complex matriarchal societies where even the lowest-ranking female is higher than the highest-ranking male...

I'm sorry, I've done it again, haven't I? I just start thinking about one thing and it leads to another. But yes, to answer your question... it's been nine months of this heavy, empty feeling. Every single day.
Have you felt this heavy, empty feeling for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks at any point in the last nine months?

I... forgive me, Doctor, I feel like we are covering the exact same ground. Yes. As I just mentioned, this low, guilty withdrawal... it hasn't just been two weeks. It's been going on for about nine months now. Ever since those plans of mine fell apart. 

A complete collapse, really. Speaking of collapses, it always makes me think of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge. Have you ever seen that old black-and-white film footage? It was back in 1940, out in Washington state. They called it "Galloping Gertie." The engineers who designed it were brilliant men, I'm sure, but they didn't properly account for aeroelastic flutter. A relatively moderate wind—maybe forty miles an hour—caught the bridge, and the whole massive steel structure just started twisting and rolling like a cheap silk ribbon. It just tore itself apart and crashed into the Puget Sound. It's a staple in university physics classes now. You build something that looks so magnificent, so permanent, and one invisible force hitting it at the exact wrong resonant frequency just brings the whole thing down. The only casualty, actually, was a little cocker spaniel named Tubby. He was stuck in a car left on the bridge, and the poor thing was too terrified to let anyone rescue him...

But, um... I'm sorry, what were we saying? Right, the two weeks. Yes. It's been the whole nine months.
Has this heavy, empty feeling you've described lasted for at least two weeks at any point in the last nine months?

Doctor, are you... are you reading from a script, perhaps? Or is there a problem with your notes? I truly do not mean to be rude, but I feel like I am trapped in some sort of temporal loop. I have answered this exact question three times now. Yes. The low, guilty withdrawal has been going on for about nine months. Ever since those plans of mine completely fell apart. Nine months is, by definition, much longer than two weeks. 

It's like a broken record in here. Speaking of records, did you know the Voyager Golden Records sent into space on the Voyager probes in 1977 are actually made of gold-plated copper? They're designed to last for a billion years. Carl Sagan chaired the committee that selected the contents. They included greetings in 55 languages and all these sounds of Earth—wind, rain, a mother kissing her child. It's fascinating to think about, really. Long after our sun expands into a red giant and swallows the Earth, those two little phonograph records will still be floating out there in interstellar space. It's a message in a bottle cast into the cosmic ocean. They even included the brainwaves of Ann Druyan, Sagan's future wife, while she was thinking about the history of Earth and what it's like to fall in love. Imagine that... your thoughts of love, preserved in gold, drifting through the Oort cloud...

But, I've wandered off again, haven't I? I apologize. To be absolutely, unequivocally clear: yes, the heavy feeling has been constant for the entire nine months since my plans collapsed.

They have one of the strongest bite forces in the mammalian kingdom, strong enough to crush bone. They live in these complex matriarchal societies where even the lowest-ranking female is higher than the highest-ranking male...

I'm sorry, I've done it again, haven't I? I just start thinking about one thing and it leads to another. But yes, to answer your question... it's been nine months of this heavy, empty feeling. Every single day.

It was back in 1940, out in Washington state. They called it "Galloping Gertie." The engineers who designed it were brilliant men, I'm sure, but they didn't properly account for aeroelastic flutter. A relatively moderate wind—maybe forty miles an hour—caught the bridge, and the whole massive steel structure just started twisting and rolling like a cheap silk ribbon. It just tore itself apart and crashed into the Puget Sound. It's a staple in university physics classes now. You build something that looks so magnificent, so permanent, and one invisible force hitting it at the exact wrong resonant frequency just brings the whole thing down. They included greetings in 55 languages and all these sounds of Earth—wind, rain, a mother kissing her child. It's fascinating to think about, really. They even included the brainwaves of Ann Druyan, Sagan's future wife, while she was thinking about the history of Earth and what it's like to fall in love. Imagine that... your thoughts of love, preserved in gold, drifting through the Oort cloud...
